claim: SARS-CoV-2 has caused over 200 million COVID-19 cases and over 4 million deaths around the world up to September 2021.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has caused over 200 million COVID-19 cases and over 4 million deaths around the world up to September 2021 (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022

claim: There is an ongoing debate whether children should be vaccinated or prioritized for vaccination against SARS-CoV-2.
source: Although vaccines have been approved, even for young children, there is an ongoing debate whether such age classes should be vaccinated or prioritized for vaccination (Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2021

claim: More infectious SARS-CoV-2 variants can cause significant outbreaks among children.
source: While the contribution of children in the COVID-19 epidemic is still subject to discussion (Gaythorpe et al., 2021), there is a consensus that more infectious variants can cause significant outbreaks among children (Milne et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milne et al., 2022

claim: Children who typically undergo SARS-CoV-2 infection with little or no symptoms might still be highly contagious and generate new infections in the community.
source: Furthermore, recent work indicates that children, who typically undergo an infection with little or no symptoms, might still be highly contagious and as such generate new infections in the community (Meuris et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meuris et al., 2021

claim: Students of age 8–11 years made less progress while learning from home during school closures.
source: In fact, Engzell et al. evaluated the impact of school closures on students' learning performance, finding that students of age 8–11 years made less progress while learning from home (Engzell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engzell et al., 2021

claim: A repetitive testing strategy reduces transmissions in a school context but increases absenteeism.
source: Several scientific investigation discussed the use of testing strategies in school settings, for example (Colosi et al., 2022; Leng et al., 2022; GOV UK, 2021a; GOV UK, 2021b; Paltiel and Schwartz, 2021; Chang et al., 2020a; Hamer et al., 2021), suggesting that a repetitive testing strategy reduces transmissions in a school context but increases absenteeism.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: Symptomatic isolation results in infection of a significant proportion of the school population for both Wuhan strain (median: 0.03, 95% quantile interval [0.01,0.04]) and Delta VoC (median: 0.14, 95% quantile interval [0.10,0.18]).
source: On the one hand, our modelling experiments (details on the simulation model in the Methods section) show (Figure 1) that symptomatic isolation results in the infection of a significant proportion of the school population (Wuhan strain, median: 0.03, 95% quantile interval [0.01,0.04]; Delta VoC, median: 0.14, 95% quantile interval [0.10,0.18]).
evidence: Supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1

claim: 80% of pupils will go through SARS-CoV-2 infection asymptomatically in the model.
source: This comes as no surprise, as in our model we assume that 80% of the pupils will go through the infection asymptomatically, and by following this testing policy, we are only able to pick up infections that make up the tip of the iceberg.
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly

claim: Repetitive testing is the strategy that most reduces the attack rate (Wuhan strain, median: 0.02, 95% quantile interval [0.01,0.03]; Delta VoC, median: 0.05, 95% quantile interval [0.04,0.07]).
source: Among the two screening options, we observe that repetitive approach is the strategy that most reduce the attack rate (Wuhan strain, median: 0.02, 95% quantile interval [0.01,0.03]; Delta VoC, median: 0.05, 95% quantile interval [0.04,0.07]).
evidence: Supported by simulation data

claim: Reactive screening strategy performs only slightly better than symptomatic isolation (Wuhan strain, median: 0.03, 95% quantile interval [0.01,0.04]; Delta VoC, median: 0.12, 95% quantile interval [0.10,0.17]).
source: However, contrary to intuition, our experiments indicate that the reactive screening strategy performs only slightly better than symptomatic isolation (Wuhan strain, median: 0.03, 95% quantile interval [0.01,0.04]; Delta VoC, median: 0.12, 95% quantile interval [0.10,0.17]).
evidence: Supported by simulation data

claim: Four asymptomatic generations take place, on average, before a symptomatic infection is observed when 80% of infections in children progress asymptomatically.
source: When we assume that 80% of infections in children progress asymptomatically, we can expect (by assuming a geometric distribution) that four asymptomatic generations take place, on average, before a symptomatic infection is observed.
evidence: Based on mathematical inference from geometric distribution

claim: Only 30% of symptomatic children are detected due to the fact that many children exhibit only minor symptoms.
source: Note that we also assume that only a limited percentage of symptomatic children is detected (30%), due to the fact that many children exhibit only minor symptoms.
evidence: This is a model assumption based on reasoning about symptom presentation

claim: For symptomatic isolation strategy, the average NSDL per child is directly proportional to the fraction of symptomatic cases (Wuhan strain, median: 0.08, 95% quantile interval [0.03,0.3]; Delta VoC, median: 0.3, 95% quantile interval [0.07,0.63]).
source: For the symptomatic isolation strategy, only children with symptoms are isolated, resulting in an average NSDL per child that is directly proportional to the fraction symptomatic cases (Wuhan strain, median: 0.08, 95% quantile interval [0.03,0.3]; Delta VoC, median: 0.3, 95% quantile interval [0.07,0.63]).
evidence: Supported by simulation data

claim: Reactive screening results in higher NSDL (Wuhan strain, median: 0.59, 95% quantile interval [0.11,1.34]; Delta VoC, median: 1.99, 95% quantile interval [0.68,11.58]) due to quickly reaching class or school closure thresholds.
source: For reactive screening, additional asymptomatic pupils might be identified, thereby quickly reaching the class or school closure thresholds, with a higher NSDL as a result (Wuhan strain, median: 0.59, 95% quantile interval [0.11,1.34]; Delta VoC, median: 1.99, 95% quantile interval [0.68,11.58]).
evidence: Supported by simulation data

claim: Repetitive testing results in very high NSDL (Wuhan strain, median: 13.85, 95% quantile interval [3.50,31.93]; Delta VoC, median: 42.18, 95% quantile interval [32.97,51.64]) due to rapidly meeting class and/or school closure thresholds.
source: This effect is most pronounced when we apply repetitive testing, where we effectively detect a high proportion of the infections, thereby rapidly meeting the class and/or school closure thresholds, with a very high NSDL as a consequence (Wuhan strain, median: 13.85, 95% quantile interval [3.50,31.93]; Delta VoC, median: 42.18, 95% quantile interval [32.97,51.64]).
evidence: Supported by simulation data

claim: By using repetitive testing, more lenient class closure thresholds could be applied with only a limited impact on the attack rate.
source: We argue that, by using repetitive testing, more lenient thresholds could be applied, as we are able to detect a larger proportion of cases. We investigate this in Figure 2 where we remove the school closure threshold, and investigate a set of class closure thresholds while considering a repetitive testing strategy. This experiment confirms that a larger class threshold can be used, with only a limited impact on the attack rate, and that such thresholds result in a more acceptable NSDL.
evidence: Supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2

claim: A more stringent school threshold shows a positive effect on controlling the attack rate but drastically increases the NSDL.
source: A more stringent school threshold shows a positive effect on controlling the attack rate, but drastically increases the NSDL (Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 9

claim: The difference between testing strategies is most pronounced in case of the more infectious virus strain (Delta VoC).
source: While the overall trends of the reported measures are similar for the Wuhan and Delta scenarios, the difference between the testing strategies is most pronounced in case of the more infectious virus strain (i.e., the Delta VoC).
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results across scenarios

claim: In the Omicron scenario with low immunity levels and a shorter incubation period, high attack rates were observed that are more difficult to control.
source: In our Omicron scenario with low immunity levels and a shorter incubation period, we observed high attack rates that are more difficult to control (Appendix 1—figure 20).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 20

claim: The impact of additional seeding cases amplifies the attack rate, but repetitive testing proved to be robust in regard of this parameter.
source: We note that the impact of additional seeding cases amplifies the attack rate, but overall repetitive testing proved to be robust in regard of this parameter (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis data in Appendix 1—figure 1

claim: A higher attack rate is detected in schools with smaller sizes when the seeding number is kept the same.
source: Futher, we notice that a higher attack rate is detected in school with smaller sizes when the seeding number is kept the same (Appendix 1—figure 17).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 17

claim: When introducing a number of seeds proportional to the school size, the attack rate and NSDL are similar, but a higher stochasticity is observed for the smaller school size.
source: When introducing a number of seeds proportional to the school size, the attack rate and NSDL are similar, but a higher stochasticity is observed for the smaller school size (Appendix 1—figure 18).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 18

claim: Asymptomatic individuals are as infectious as symptomatic individuals, as recently observed by Meuris et al., 2021.
source: Next, we assume that asymptomatic individuals are as infectious as symptomatic individuals, as recently observed by Meuris et al., 2021.
evidence: Supported by citation to Meuris et al., 2021

claim: Repetitive testing and reactive screening are less effective when the turnaround time is increased.
source: Repetitive testing and reactive screening are less effective when the turnaround time is increased (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 15

claim: Reactive screening performs similar to symptomatic isolation for a turnaround time of 3 days, but repetitive screening is still the most successful strategy to reduce the number of infections.
source: While reactive screening performs similar to symptomatic isolation for a turnaround time of 3 days, repetitive screening is still the strategy that is most successful to reduce the number of infections.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results

claim: Testing strategies show a lower performance when a shorter incubation period is considered.
source: In addition, testing strategies show a lower performance when a shorter incubation period is considered (Appendix 1—figure 14).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 14

claim: Testing the entire school population twice per week squashes a highly contagious epidemic such as driven by the Delta VoC.
source: We also consider a repetitive testing scenario where we test the entire school population twice per week, which shows that such a strategy squashes a highly contagious epidemic such as driven by the Delta VoC (Appendix 1—figures 2 and 3)
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figures 2 and 3

claim: Testing twice per week reduces the attack rate of an immune-evasive VoC with shorter incubation period, as the Omicron VoC.
source: We also consider a repetitive testing scenario where we test the entire school population twice per week, which shows that such a strategy squashes a highly contagious epidemic such as driven by the Delta VoC (Appendix 1—figures 2 and 3) and reduces the attack rate of an immune-evasive VoC with shorter incubation period, as the Omicron VoC (Appendix 1—figure 21).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 21

claim: Attack rate decreases and NSDL increases when compliance to repetitive testing is increased.
source: Considering a repetitive testing strategy, we also tested the compliance to testing, showing that attack rate decreases and NSDL increases when compliance is increased (Appendix 1—figure 16).
evidence: Supported by simulation data in Appendix 1—figure 16

claim: In the experimental setting, a compliance of 60% leads to a similar attack rate as a compliance of 100%.
source: Interestingly, in our experimental setting, a compliance of 60% leads to a similar attack rate than a compliance of 100%.
evidence: Supported by simulation data

claim: The low efficacy of symptomatic testing and reactive screening procedures is explained by the asymptomatic nature of SARS-CoV-2 infections, especially for children.
source: The low efficacy of the symptomatic testing and reactive screening procedures is explained by the asymptomatic nature of SARS-CoV-2 infections, especially for children.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results and known characteristics of infection

claim: When surveillance is based just on the onset of symptoms, asymptomatic carriers avoid detection and intervention, sustaining the spread of the virus.
source: In fact, when surveillance is based just on the onset of symptoms, asymptomatic carriers avoid detection and intervention, sustaining the spread of the virus.
evidence: Based on logical inference from model structure and results

claim: Repetitive testing can keep transmission under control and limit the number of school days lost when no school or class thresholds are considered.
source: Within our experimental settings, we observe that repetitive testing can keep transmission under control and limit the number of school days lost.
evidence: Supported by simulation data

claim: A class pooling approach could be used to reduce the number of PCR samples to be analyzed.
source: To make this procedure more efficient, a class pooling approach could be used to reduce the number of samples to be analyzed (Libin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Libin et al., 2021

claim: Teachers are allocated to specific classes and are assumed to interact only with individuals with whom they share the same class.
source: We assume that teachers are allocated to specific classes and are assumed to interact only with individuals with whom they share the same class.
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly

claim: The assumption that teachers interact only within their classes is reasonable at this stage of the epidemic, where a large proportion of teachers is either immune or vaccinated.
source: We argue that this is a reasonable assumption at this stage of the epidemic, where a large proportion of teachers is either immune or vaccinated.
evidence: Based on reasoning about epidemic context

claim: The threshold for participating in saliva sampling is low.
source: We argue that this is a reasonable assumption, as the threshold for participating in saliva sampling is low, and societal awareness and support for this policies can be achieved, via prompt governmental communication.
evidence: Based on reasoning about practical aspects of saliva sampling

claim: Symptomatic individuals develop symptoms at the peak of their infectiousness.
source: We assume that symptomatic individuals develop symptoms at the peak of their infectiousness, at which they can be detected and placed in isolation for 10 days.
evidence: This is a model assumption

claim: All testing policies will close a class when the number of infections in this class exceeds two cases.
source: All testing policies will close a class when the number of infections in this class exceeds two cases.
evidence: This is a model assumption

claim: All testing policies will close the school when the number of infections over all classes exceeds 20 cases.
source: Analogously, all testing policies will close the school when the number of infections over all classes exceeds 20 cases.
evidence: This is a model assumption

claim: When the class or school threshold is triggered, the respective class or the entire school is closed for 10 days.
source: When the class, or school, threshold is triggered, the respective class, or the entire school, is closed for 10 days.
evidence: This is a model assumption

claim: The length of isolation and of class/school closure is set according to viral clearance observations and in line with isolation policies in place in European countries in the first half of 2021.
source: The length of isolation and of class/school closure is set according to viral clearance observations (Chang et al., 2020b), and in line with isolation policies in place in European countries in the first half of 2021.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b and reference to European policies

claim: Infection counts are recorded in a 14-day time window to determine class and school closures.
source: Infection counts are recorded in a 14-day time window to determine class and school closures.
evidence: This is a model assumption

claim: Children are set to be half as susceptible as adults.
source: Children are set to be halve as susceptible as adults (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: Model parameter informed by citation to Davies et al., 2020

claim: 30% of school children are immune due to prior infection.
source: We assume that 30% of school children are immune due to prior infection, and that 90% of the teachers are immune, due to their vaccination status or due to prior infection (Sciensano, 2022).
evidence: Model assumption informed by citation to Sciensano, 2022

claim: 90% of the teachers are immune, due to their vaccination status or due to prior infection.
source: We assume that 30% of school children are immune due to prior infection, and that 90% of the teachers are immune, due to their vaccination status or due to prior infection (Sciensano, 2022).
evidence: Model assumption informed by citation to Sciensano, 2022

claim: The sensitivity of PCR tests on saliva or throat washing samples is set to 86%.
source: The sensitivity of such tests is set to 86%, and there is a one day delay in reporting the result (Butler-Laporte et al., 2021).
evidence: Model parameter informed by citation to Butler-Laporte et al., 2021

claim: There is a one day delay in reporting PCR test results.
source: The sensitivity of such tests is set to 86%, and there is a one day delay in reporting the result (Butler-Laporte et al., 2021).
evidence: Model parameter informed by citation to Butler-Laporte et al., 2021

claim: The performance of saliva sampling in combination with PCR testing is on par with nasopharyngeal swab sampling in combination with PCR testing.
source: Recent reports show that the performance of saliva sampling in combination with PCR testing is on par with nasopharyngeal swab sampling in combination with PCR testing (Wyllie et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wyllie et al., 2020

claim: Infectious individuals become PCR detectable 2 days after infection.
source: Infectious individuals become PCR detectable 2 days after infection, as previously assumed (Torneri et al., 2020; Torneri et al., 2021).
evidence: Model assumption supported by citations to Torneri et al., 2020 and Torneri et al., 2021

claim: For the reactive screening testing policy, there is a one day screening delay.
source: For the reactive screening testing policy, we assume that there is a one day screening delay.
evidence: This is a model assumption

claim: Every simulated week, five susceptible children are assumed to acquire infection outside the school environment.
source: Every simulated week, five susceptible children are assumed to acquire infection outside the school environment, accounting for disease importation or seeding.
evidence: This is a model assumption

claim: The epidemic is simulated for 100 days.
source: The epidemic is simulated for 100 days and we consider an ensemble of 100 simulation runs to present our final results.
evidence: This is a model parameter

claim: An ensemble of 100 simulation runs is used to present the final results.
source: The epidemic is simulated for 100 days and we consider an ensemble of 100 simulation runs to present our final results.
evidence: This is a model parameter

claim: The attack rate is defined as the total number of cases (minus the index cases) divided by the number of pupils in the school.
source: The former is defined as the total number of cases (minus the index cases) divided by the the number of pupils in the school, and we refer to this quantity as the attack rate.
evidence: This is a definition of a model output measure

claim: The number of school days lost (NSDL) is defined as the sum of the school day lost divided by the school size.
source: The latter is defined as the sum of the school day lost divided by the school size, and we refer to this quantity as number of school days lost (NSDL).
evidence: This is a definition of a model output measure

claim: Repetitive testing strategies can significantly reduce the attack rate in schools, contrary to a reactive screening or a symptomatic isolation approach.
source: Through this analysis, we demonstrate that repetitive testing strategies can significantly reduce the attack rate in schools, contrary to a reactive screening or a symptomatic isolation approach.
evidence: Supported by simulation data presented in the study

claim: When a repetitive testing strategy is in place, more cases will be detected and class and school closures are more easily triggered, leading to a higher number of school days lost per child.
source: However, when a repetitive testing strategy is in place, more cases will be detected and class and school closures are more easily triggered, leading to a higher number of school days lost per child.
evidence: Supported by simulation data presented in the study

claim: While maintaining the epidemic under control with a repetitive testing strategy, absenteeism can be reduced by relaxing class and school closure thresholds.
source: While maintaining the epidemic under control with a repetitive testing strategy, we show that absenteeism can be reduced by relaxing class and school closure thresholds.
evidence: Supported by simulation data presented in the study
